items.title: L10: A ministerial direction step by step
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money, Annex 3.1 (Accounting Officer ministerial directions); Accounting Officer System Statement
items.body: A ministerial direction is the formal mechanism by which a minister can proceed with a policy that the accounting officer has advised does not meet one of the four standards. The sequence matters. First, the accounting officer identifies the concern, usually in a submission, and sets out why the proposal may fail regularity, propriety, value for money or feasibility. The minister may reconsider, amend the proposal or accept the advice. If the minister still wants to proceed, the accounting officer asks for a written direction. The minister must give it in writing, setting out their reasons and recognising that they have chosen to override the advice. The accounting officer then carries out the direction, unless it concerns regularity or propriety in a way that makes the spending unlawful, because an accounting officer cannot lawfully act beyond the authority Parliament has given. Within the guidance, the practice is that an accounting officer can ask for a direction on regularity or propriety, but a direction cannot make an unlawful payment lawful. For concerns about value for money or feasibility, a direction can be given and followed. After a direction, the department sends a copy to the Comptroller and Auditor General, who can report the matter to Parliament, and the Public Accounts Committee may examine it. The Treasury is also informed, and the direction is published, with the accounting officer's letter, usually after a short time. The effect is to transfer visible responsibility to the minister. It does not stop the accounting officer from being asked about the decision, and they should keep the paper trail. Directions are rare and signal serious disagreement, so many disputes are resolved earlier through discussion. An accounting officer should also consider whether to use them for feasibility, which relates to delivery and timelines.

questions.prompt: The minister rejects an accounting officer's written advice about value for money and wishes to proceed. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: The minister signs off the spending, the officer informs the press and the Treasury cancels the scheme
The officer declines to comply, the minister overrules in Parliament and the C&AG approves it
Written direction requested, minister gives reasons, officer complies, copy sent to the C&AG
The officer refers the matter to the Civil Service Commission, which decides whether to proceed

questions.hint: The direction is written, followed and copied to the C&AG.

questions.prompt: An accounting officer receives a direction on a proposal that would be unlawful because Parliament gave no authority for the payment. What follows?

options.text: The accounting officer must carry it out, because the direction transfers all responsibility to the minister
The Treasury will approve the spending retrospectively once the direction is issued
The accounting officer carries it out but records the disagreement in the accounts
The direction cannot make the spending lawful, so the accounting officer should not carry it out

questions.prompt: Why do directions on feasibility tend to be more common than other types?

options.text: Feasibility is about delivery risk, where officials and ministers often differ
Feasibility is the only test on which an accounting officer is allowed to ask for a direction
Feasibility concerns are decided by the National Audit Office rather than the department
Feasibility is outside Treasury rules, so it cannot support a direction

questions.prompt: What is the main effect of a ministerial direction on accountability?

options.text: It removes the accounting officer's duty to account to Parliament for the spending concerned
It makes the minister visibly responsible for overriding the advice
It makes the Comptroller and Auditor General responsible for the decision to proceed
It moves responsibility for the spending from the department to the Treasury

questions.hint: Direction clarifies who chose the risk.

questions.prompt: After a direction is issued, who sees it?

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General and the Treasury, with publication following
Only the minister and the permanent secretary, to keep the dispute within the department
Only the department's board, which then decides whether to publish it
The Cabinet Secretary alone, who decides if anyone else should see it

questions.hint: Directions are shared with the C&AG and Treasury.

questions.prompt: An accounting officer wants a direction after a minister verbally says to proceed. Which is the correct next step?

options.text: Accept the verbal instruction and note it on the file, since the minister is clearly responsible
Insist on a written direction setting out the minister's reasons before acting
Proceed, then ask the minister to confirm afterwards by email
Proceed once the private office has said that the minister agrees

questions.hint: A direction must be in writing.

questions.prompt: A permanent secretary suggests that every disagreement about policy should go to a direction. Why is this a poor approach?

options.text: Directions are for any serious policy disagreement, so using them often is normal
Directions can only be used by the Treasury, not by departmental accounting officers
Directions concern the four standards, not policy disagreements, and are rare
Directions stop ministers taking any decision the accounting officer questions

questions.hint: Use directions only where the standards are engaged.

questions.prompt: What should officials supporting the accounting officer do throughout?

options.text: Wait until the direction is signed before writing down the advice that was given
Share the advice with the press office so that it can prepare handling lines
Record only the minister's final decision, not the advice that preceded it
Keep a clear paper trail of advice, the minister's response and the direction

items.title: L10: Pre-election dilemmas in combination
items.source: Cabinet Office, General Election Guidance; Cabinet Manual
items.body: The pre-election period raises problems that need judgement rather than a simple rule. Officials weigh three things: the need for government to continue, the duty not to affect the election, and the risk of binding a successor. Take a department due to publish a report on a long-running programme during the period. If the report is a routine statutory publication with a fixed date, it usually goes ahead, perhaps with the foreword adjusted to avoid party-political content. If the report is discretionary and would be controversial, delay is likely. A department preparing to launch a consultation might wait, unless the consultation is legally required. Contracts: if a contract is time-critical and delay would cause significant cost or harm, a decision may go ahead, with consideration of break clauses to avoid binding an incoming government. Where a decision could be taken by the next government at little cost, officials will advise to wait. Appointments to public bodies are generally paused if they are not urgent. Ministers who remain in post continue to take decisions needed for the running of the department, but they exercise restraint, and the Cabinet Secretary may be consulted on difficult cases. Officials must treat opposition parties fairly, for example in handling information requests or access talks, and avoid using public resources to the advantage of the governing party. Questions and answers on policy continue, and the official Parliamentary and press offices maintain a reduced operation. If an event, such as an emergency, arises, government acts as required. Throughout, the aim is to keep faith with both continuity and the neutrality of the Civil Service. Records of decisions taken, and reasons, are kept because they may be scrutinised after the election.

questions.prompt: A statutory report has a legally fixed publication date inside the pre-election period. What is the usual approach?

options.text: Publish it later, after the election, since the law allows a short delay for any report
Publish it on the date, checking the text for party-political content
Publish it on the date, but with a foreword from the minister praising the programme
Publish it only if the main opposition party has agreed to the timing

questions.prompt: A discretionary report that would be controversial is ready. What does the guidance suggest?

options.text: Publish it, because delay would itself look political and damage trust in the department
Publish it with a covering statement from the governing party explaining its context
Send it to the opposition first so they can respond on the day
Delay it, as it could affect the election and is not required to be published now

questions.hint: Discretionary controversial items are usually delayed.

questions.prompt: A time-critical contract needs to be signed during the period, and delay would cause significant harm. Which is the best way to proceed?

options.text: Decide if justified, using break clauses so a successor is not locked in
Refuse to sign any contract during the period, whatever the cost of delay
Sign it, including a clause that prevents any later government reviewing it
Sign it only with the opposition's consent, so that it is not seen as partisan

questions.prompt: A minister's request to launch a non-statutory consultation falls in the period. What is the usual advice?

options.text: Launch it, because consultations are neutral and do not commit a government
Launch it, but shorten the closing date so it ends before polling day
Wait until after the election unless a legal or urgent reason applies
Launch it and invite the opposition parties to respond first

questions.hint: Consultations on new policy can bind a successor.

questions.prompt: Why do officials keep records of decisions taken during the period?

options.text: Because the opposition has a right to see each decision before it is taken
Decisions may be scrutinised later, so reasons must be clear
Because the Cabinet Secretary must approve every decision in the period
Because decisions must be published daily while the period lasts

questions.prompt: An emergency occurs during the period. What is the right approach?

options.text: Government waits until a new government has been formed before taking any decision
Decisions are delegated to the opposition spokespeople for the duration
Government acts as required, using normal decision-making with care for neutrality
The Cabinet Secretary takes over as Prime Minister until the result is known

questions.prompt: Which question helps decide whether a decision should proceed?

options.text: Will it help the governing party at the election?
Will it be noticed by the press?
Is it popular with the voters in marginal constituencies?
Could it wait for a new government without harm?

questions.prompt: How should officials handle requests from the opposition for information during the period?

options.text: Treat them fairly, without advantage to the governing party
Refuse every request until after the election, to avoid any suggestion of favour
Give the governing party advance sight of every request received
Respond only if the Prime Minister has approved the reply

items.title: L10: A function moves: who answers for what
items.source: Cabinet Office, Machinery of government changes; Managing Public Money; Statement of Practice on staff transfers
items.body: Imagine that a function, with an arm's length body that carries it out, moves from Department A to Department B. Several accountabilities shift, and some do not. The move is made by the Prime Minister's decision and given legal effect by an order transferring functions between ministers. From the effective date, the Secretary of State in Department B is accountable to Parliament for the policy and for sponsoring the body; the Secretary of State in Department A is no longer answerable for it. Department B's permanent secretary becomes responsible for assurance about the body, and, if the body's chief executive is its accounting officer, that remains true, with the body's accountability now to Department B. The Estimates must reflect the new allocation of money, so Parliament's authority follows the function. Staff in the transferring team move to Department B, with their terms protected under the Statement of Practice, but the body's own staff continue as before. Existing legal rights and obligations, such as contracts, transfer, and the receiving department takes on associated liabilities, so a thorough assessment of risks, litigation and commitments is needed. Handover should include a risk register, key contacts, outstanding decisions, correspondence and data. Parliamentary scrutiny shifts, so select committee interest may change, and outstanding parliamentary questions are transferred. The body's framework document must be revised to name the new sponsor. For a period, officials in Department A may need to support Department B, under a clear arrangement. Public information must also be updated. Where a transfer occurs mid-year, the department that previously spent the money keeps its past accounts, and the new one reports from the transfer date. The change does not alter the body's own legal status or independence.

questions.prompt: From the transfer date, which minister answers to Parliament for the body's sponsorship?

options.text: The Secretary of State of Department B
The Secretary of State of Department A until the end of the financial year
Both Secretaries of State jointly, for a transitional year
The Prime Minister, who made the decision to move the function

questions.prompt: What happens to a contract held by Department A for the function?

options.text: It ends on transfer and must be retendered by the new department
It stays with Department A, which keeps managing it for the new owner
It transfers, with the associated rights and liabilities
It is held by the Treasury until a new supplier is chosen

questions.prompt: Which document must be revised after the move?

options.text: The Civil Service Code, which must be updated for each sponsored body
The body's framework document, to name the new sponsor
The Public Records Act, which names the sponsor of each public body
The body's Royal Charter, in every case, which has to be reissued

questions.prompt: Why must the Estimates reflect the move?

options.text: Because the Treasury insists on a new budget cycle each time a function moves
Because the minister must approve each line of the new department's budget
Because the body must be audited again after a transfer
Parliament votes money to departments, so authority follows the function

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the body's chief executive after the move?

options.text: They remain the accounting officer, now answerable within Department B's framework
They become a civil servant in Department B and stop being the body's accounting officer
They stop being accountable for spending until the next financial year
They report to the Treasury only, rather than to the sponsor department

questions.prompt: Why is a thorough risk and liability assessment needed before handover?

options.text: The Treasury will pay any liabilities, so the receiving department need not assess them
The receiving department takes on associated liabilities and commitments
The old department keeps all liabilities, whatever the contract says
Liabilities end at the date of transfer, so no assessment is needed

questions.prompt: What should handover to Department B include?

options.text: Only the staff list, since other matters are dealt with by the Treasury
Only the budget figures, as risks stay with the old department
A risk register, contacts, open decisions, correspondence and data
Only the press releases, so that announcements can be reissued

questions.prompt: What happens to outstanding parliamentary questions on the function?

options.text: They lapse when the function moves and are not answered
The old department must answer them for the rest of the session
They are answered by the Speaker's office
They are transferred to the new department to answer

items.title: L10: A policy that crosses devolved boundaries
items.source: Cabinet Office, Devolution guidance notes; Scotland Act 1998; Government of Wales Act 2006; Intergovernmental relations framework
items.body: Consider a UK department that wants to legislate on a subject which is partly reserved and partly devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Several issues arise at once. First, the officials must work out which parts of the subject are reserved and which are devolved in each nation, because the settlements differ. Second, if the Bill touches devolved matters in a way that engages the Sewel convention, the UK Government normally seeks legislative consent from each devolved legislature. This requires early engagement, shared drafts, and time for the devolved governments to consult their legislatures and take a view. Third, where a devolved legislature withholds consent, the UK Parliament may still legislate, but doing so is politically significant and breaks the convention, so ministers must decide with their eyes open. Fourth, funding must be considered. If UK spending on a comparable devolved service in England changes, the Barnett formula adjusts the devolved block grants, and policy design may need to consider consequential funding. Fifth, interactions may be handled through common frameworks, which are agreements on how to manage divergence in specific areas. Sixth, the UK Government must be careful about announcing the policy for England only, as GOV.UK and press material must be clear about territorial extent, to avoid misleading the public. Seventh, officials in each government serve their own ministers, so confidentiality about drafts must be agreed, while recognising that devolved governments may be led by different parties. If disagreements cannot be resolved at official level, they go to the intergovernmental forum at ministerial level. Throughout, impartiality and honesty require officials to avoid misrepresenting what the other governments have agreed.

questions.prompt: A UK Bill touches a devolved area in Wales. What should the UK Government normally do?

options.text: Seek the Senedd's legislative consent, engaging early with the Welsh Government
Ignore the Senedd, because the UK Parliament is sovereign and the convention is only advisory
Ask the Welsh Government to approve the Bill's wording line by line
Wait until the Bill has become an Act and then ask the Senedd to consent

questions.prompt: A devolved legislature refuses consent. What is the position?

options.text: The Bill falls automatically, because consent is a legal requirement
The Supreme Court must decide whether the Bill can proceed
It can still legislate, but breaks the convention at political cost
The Bill can then apply only in England

questions.hint: Consent is a convention, not a legal veto.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism manages divergence in areas where devolved and UK rules interact?

options.text: Parliamentary privilege, which allows Parliament to set rules for its members
Common frameworks
Judicial review, which allows the courts to resolve differences between governments
Collective responsibility, which binds ministers to a common position

questions.prompt: A press notice announces a new scheme without saying it covers England only. What is the problem?

options.text: None, as UK press notices are assumed to cover the whole UK
It breaches the Official Secrets Act, since it reveals extent
It breaches only the Ministerial Code, not the Civil Service Code
It risks misleading the public about territorial extent

questions.prompt: Why does the Barnett formula matter to policy design?

options.text: It sets income tax rates in each nation, which alters policy design
It decides which Bills need legislative consent from devolved legislatures
Spending changes in England can bring consequentials for devolved budgets
It sets the number of MPs each nation sends to Westminster

questions.prompt: Officials in the UK and Scottish governments share a draft. How should confidentiality be handled?

options.text: Agree handling rules in advance, recognising each serves its own ministers
Assume everything is public, because the governments are part of one UK system
Share it with the press, so each nation can comment on it
Avoid sharing drafts at all, since the governments serve different ministers

questions.prompt: A disagreement cannot be resolved by officials. What is the next stage?

options.text: Referral to the Civil Service Commission, which settles disputes between governments
A referendum in the nations affected
Referral to the Speaker of the House of Commons
Escalation to ministerial level through intergovernmental forums

questions.prompt: What is the first analytical step when the subject is partly reserved and partly devolved?

options.text: Draft the Bill in full, then see which nations object
Establish what is reserved and devolved in each nation
Announce the policy and then check the legal position
Ask the Treasury to decide which nations are covered

items.title: L10: A request that raises FOI, data protection and security together
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; UK GDPR; Government Security Classifications Policy
items.body: Some requests engage several regimes at once, and officials have to decide which applies and in what order. Imagine a request for a report, held on a claimant management system, about complaints made by named staff about a supplier's data handling, some of it marked Official-Sensitive. First, identify the type of request. If the requester asks about their own personal data, it is a subject access request under UK GDPR; if they ask about information in general, it is a Freedom of Information request, or an Environmental Information request if the information is environmental. Second, consider the content. Personal data of third parties, such as staff names, is exempt under FOI if its disclosure would breach data protection principles, which involves weighing legitimate interests against the individuals' rights and expectations. Senior staff acting in public roles may have lower expectations of privacy than junior staff. Third, consider other exemptions: commercial interests of the supplier, which are qualified and require a public interest test; security matters, which may need a specialist view; and the safe space for policy discussions. Fourth, the security classification is a guide to handling, not an exemption; marking something Official-Sensitive does not decide whether it can be released under the Act, so the content has to be assessed. Fifth, consider whether part of the report can be released with redactions. Sixth, record the reasoning, because the decision may go to internal review, the ICO and the Tribunal. Seventh, ensure that any release does not itself create a data breach, for example by metadata that reveals hidden information. Throughout, the time limit of 20 working days runs from receipt, though more time may be taken for the public interest test where the Act allows, and the requester should be told.

questions.prompt: A report is marked Official-Sensitive. What does this mean for an FOI request?

options.text: The marking guides handling; it does not decide release
The report is exempt automatically, because of the marking
The report must be released automatically, since the marking is only a guide
The report can be released only with the Cabinet Secretary's authority

questions.prompt: A requester asks for a copy of data held about themselves in the system. Which regime applies?

options.text: A freedom of information request, because the information is held by the department
An environmental information request, since the data is held electronically
Subject access under UK GDPR
A request under the Official Secrets Act, because the claimant has the right to know

questions.prompt: Staff names appear in the report. Which factor affects whether the names can be released?

options.text: Whether the staff member has agreed to their name being used in the report
Whether release would breach the data protection principles
Whether the names are already in the department's internal directory
Whether the requester is a journalist with a public interest purpose

questions.prompt: Which consideration usually makes senior staff names easier to release than junior staff names?

options.text: Senior staff are always willing to be named, whatever their role
Junior staff are not covered by data protection law at all
Senior staff are not covered by data protection law because of their pay
Senior staff in public roles may have lower expectations of privacy

questions.prompt: Part of the report is commercially sensitive but the rest is not. What is the best approach?

options.text: Withhold the whole report, because part of it is sensitive
Release the whole report, since the Act favours disclosure
Redact the sensitive part and release the rest
Ask the supplier to rewrite the sensitive part before release

questions.prompt: Why should the reasoning be recorded?

options.text: The decision may go to internal review, the ICO and the Tribunal
The supplier will ask to see the reasoning before it is released
It is required by the Public Records Act whenever a request is refused
The Speaker may ask for the reasoning in the Commons

questions.prompt: What risk can arise when releasing electronic documents?

options.text: The file may be too big for the requester's email system
Hidden metadata may reveal unintended information
Recipients may print the document and pass it on
The requester may alter the document after release

questions.prompt: The public interest test takes longer than 20 working days. What should the department do?

options.text: Ignore the limit, because the public interest test overrides it
Refuse the request, since the limit cannot be extended
Release everything now so that the limit is not breached
Say more time is needed for the public interest test

questions.hint: Extension is permitted for the test.

items.title: L10: A conflict of interest that grows
items.source: Civil Service Code; Managing Public Money; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: Conflicts of interest are rarely one-off events; they grow as circumstances change. Imagine an official who joins a procurement team and, early on, declares that their brother works for one of the possible bidders. The manager agrees a safeguard: the official will not score that bidder's tender. Later, the official is asked to take part in the pre-market engagement, where bidders ask questions. At the same time the brother invites them to a family event where the bidder's directors will be present. Next, the official hears that a rival bidder has complained about the process. The right course involves several steps. First, a declaration is a living record, so the official should update it and discuss the new situation with their manager at each stage, rather than treating the first safeguard as covering everything. Second, the safeguard should be reassessed: involvement in market engagement might give the bidder access to the official, so it may be wise to move the official off the project entirely or to limit contact. Third, any hospitality or social event should be assessed against the Code and the rules on gifts and hospitality; attending a family event is not in itself improper, but the presence of the bidder's directors means the official should declare and consider whether to attend. Fourth, the complaint from the rival bidder means that the record of how the conflict was managed will be tested, so contemporaneous notes are important. Fifth, transparency to colleagues on the panel prevents later claims of undue influence. Sixth, the manager has a duty to manage, record and review the arrangement. The principle is that the more serious the risk to the integrity or appearance of the process, the stronger the safeguard needed, up to withdrawal.

questions.prompt: The brother of a procurement official works for a bidder. Early on, the official agrees not to score that bidder. Later the official is asked to join market engagement events. What should happen?

options.text: Nothing further, because the original safeguard was agreed at the start of the project
Update the declaration and reassess whether the safeguard is still enough
The official should continue but avoid speaking to the bidder's staff
The official should say nothing, since the brother is not the bidder

questions.prompt: The brother invites the official to a family event where the bidder's directors will be. What is the most sensible course?

options.text: Attend without comment, since a family event is private
Decline the invitation without telling anyone why
Declare it and ask the manager whether to attend
Attend but avoid speaking to the directors

questions.prompt: A rival bidder complains about the process. Why do notes made at the time matter?

options.text: They are required by the rival bidder to prove that the process was fair
They stop any complaint from being made about the process
They replace the need for a panel to record its scores
They show how the conflict was managed when the process is tested

questions.prompt: Which principle best guides how strong the safeguard should be?

options.text: The greater the risk to the process, the stronger the safeguard
The same safeguard applies to every conflict, whatever the risk
Safeguards are needed only for officials at senior grades
The safeguard should match the official's grade, not the risk

questions.prompt: Why might it be wise to move the official off the project entirely?

options.text: Later contact with bidders could compromise the process
The brother would be offended if the official stayed involved
The official has shown they cannot be trusted with the work
The panel would be too large with the official on it

questions.prompt: Who has a duty to manage, record and review the arrangement?

options.text: The rival bidder, who has an interest in a fair process
The Treasury, which sets the rules on procurement conflicts
The brother, who knows most about the bidder
The official's manager, with the official's cooperation

questions.prompt: What does transparency to the panel prevent?

options.text: Any need for scoring by the panel
Later claims of undue influence or concealed involvement
Changes of panel membership during the process
The need for any declaration at all

questions.prompt: Which is wrong in this situation?

options.text: Updating the declaration when circumstances change
Discussing the invitation with the manager
Treating the first safeguard as permanent whatever happens later
Keeping notes of the decisions about the conflict

items.title: L10: What the Code requires when asked to mislead Parliament
items.source: Civil Service Code; Ministerial Code; Cabinet Manual
items.body: A difficult test of the Civil Service Code is when an official is asked, directly or by implication, to help give Parliament a misleading impression. Imagine that an official is drafting a written answer on the rate of a problem. The true figure is poor, but a minister's adviser suggests choosing a narrow definition that produces a better number and omitting a note on the definition. The answer would be literally accurate. Several parts of the Code apply. Honesty requires that civil servants do not deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament or others about what the department has done or is doing. Objectivity requires that they do not ignore inconvenient facts. Integrity requires that they do not act in a way that conflicts with the Code, and says that they must report breaches. The official's first step is to make the issue clear to the private office and policy lead: explain that the proposed wording would leave a false impression, and offer alternatives, such as giving the figure on the standard definition together with the narrower figure and an explanation. If the minister's office insists, the official raises the matter with a senior official, such as the director or permanent secretary, who may speak to the minister. The Ministerial Code also states that ministers should not knowingly mislead Parliament, so the minister may be receptive when the risk is explained. If the pressure continues and the answer would be sent, the Civil Service Code procedures apply: report to the nominated officer, with the Civil Service Commission as a last resort. Throughout, the official keeps a record of what was said and advised. They do not leak the draft, and they do not rewrite the answer in secret. They avoid putting their own name to the misleading wording. Often the matter is resolved through early, calm advice.

questions.prompt: A minister's adviser suggests a narrow definition that gives a better figure, with no note explaining the definition. What is the core problem?

options.text: A literally accurate answer can still mislead, which the Code forbids
The wording would be inaccurate, because a narrow definition changes the facts
The wording breaches only the Ministerial Code, so officials have no duty to act
The adviser has no right to comment on departmental answers to Parliament

questions.hint: Impression matters as well as accuracy.

questions.prompt: What is the official's best first response to the suggestion?

options.text: Quietly redraft the answer using the standard definition and send it on without comment
Send the answer as the adviser suggested and put concerns in a note to file afterwards
Decline to draft any answer on the subject until the adviser withdraws the suggestion
Explain the risk and offer wording giving both figures with an explanation

questions.hint: Calm early advice with an alternative often resolves it.

questions.prompt: The minister's office insists on the narrow wording. What is the next sensible step?

options.text: Tell the opposition, so that Parliament knows about the pressure
Send the draft to a journalist so the issue is exposed before publication
Raise it with a senior official such as the director or permanent secretary
Wait until the answer is published and then raise concerns under the Code

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code values does omitting the context most clearly engage?

options.text: Impartiality alone, since an adviser is involved
Honesty and objectivity
Integrity alone, as a conflict of interest has arisen
None of the values, since the figures given would all be accurate

questions.prompt: Why might the minister listen when the risk is explained clearly?

options.text: The Civil Service Code binds ministers to follow officials' advice on wording
The Speaker reviews each written answer before it is published
Officials can overrule a minister's choice of wording on answers to Parliament
The Ministerial Code says ministers should not knowingly mislead Parliament

questions.hint: Shared standards make the conversation easier.

questions.prompt: Which action should the official avoid?

options.text: Keeping a note of what was said and advised
Rewriting the answer in secret or leaking the draft
Seeking confidential advice from the nominated officer
Offering the private office alternative wording

questions.hint: Covert action undermines trust and the Code.

questions.prompt: If pressure continues and the answer is about to be sent, what applies?

options.text: Report straight to the Civil Service Commission, bypassing the department's routes
Report to the Speaker, who supervises answers to Parliament
Report to the nominated officer, with the Commission as a last resort
Report to the press, so that the public can judge for itself

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of what was said and advised?

options.text: It shows what the official did and supports any later explanation of events
It lets the minister be blamed if the answer is later criticised
The Speaker requires it for every written answer to a question
It replaces the need to raise the concern with anyone senior

items.title: L10: Whistleblowing: a multi-stage case
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission guidance
items.body: Imagine an official who notices that a team is recording payments as correct when they have not been checked, in order to meet a target. The official acts in stages. First, they gather facts without breaching rules: they note what they saw, when and what it appeared to show, and avoid copying large volumes of data or accessing systems outside their normal duties, which could itself breach the rules and data protection. Second, they raise the concern with their line manager, unless the manager is involved, in which case they go to another senior manager or the nominated officer. Third, they keep a record of the date and the response. Fourth, if nothing is done, they escalate to the department's whistleblowing route, which may involve an investigation by internal audit or a specialist team. At every stage, the department must treat the matter confidentially and protect the individual from detriment. Fifth, if the official is not satisfied that the department has dealt with it, they can go to the Civil Service Commission, which can consider whether the Code was breached and make recommendations. If a person believes they are suffering detriment for raising a concern, they can also seek advice on their rights under the Public Interest Disclosure Act, and may take a claim to an employment tribunal, with time limits that are short, usually three months less a day from the act complained of. A disclosure to a regulator, such as the National Audit Office for fraud involving public money, may also be a protected disclosure if conditions are met. The official should take advice from a union or independent adviser before external disclosure. Meanwhile, the department should look into the matter promptly, correct any wrongly recorded payments, and learn from it.

questions.prompt: An official notices payments recorded as checked when they were not. What is the best first step?

options.text: Note what they saw and when, without breaking any rules
Copy a large number of records to prove the problem beyond doubt
Confront the colleagues responsible, to hear their explanation
Tell the press, since the problem involves public money

questions.prompt: The line manager seems involved in the practice. Who should the official approach?

options.text: The same line manager again, in case they respond differently
The colleagues' families, who may influence them
Another senior manager or the nominated officer
The supplier concerned, who may know more about the practice

questions.prompt: Why should the official avoid accessing systems outside their normal duties to find more evidence?

options.text: It would be slow, and the official has other work to do
It is allowed if the cause is good
It would annoy colleagues, which is the main concern
It could itself breach the rules and data protection

questions.hint: Do not create a new breach.

questions.prompt: Which body can consider whether the Civil Service Code was breached if the department has not resolved the concern?

options.text: The Treasury, which oversees departmental conduct
The Civil Service Commission
The Speaker, who supervises civil servants' behaviour
The Cabinet Office press team

questions.hint: The Commission is the last stage.

questions.prompt: An official believes they are suffering detriment for raising a concern. What can they do?

options.text: Do nothing, because treatment of that kind is lawful if the department followed its process
Take advice on their rights under the Public Interest Disclosure Act, within the tribunal time limits
Ask the minister to intervene in the case, since ministers can overrule managers
Wait for the matter to resolve itself, since tribunals take a long time to hear claims

questions.hint: Rights exist with short time limits.

questions.prompt: Why should an official take independent advice before external disclosure?

options.text: The Code requires independent advice before every disclosure
External disclosure is banned in all circumstances
Unions must approve any disclosure before it is made
To understand legal risks and protection before acting

questions.prompt: Which action should the department take once the matter is raised?

options.text: Investigate the person who raised the concern, to test their motives
Wait for the end of the quarter before looking into it
Look into it promptly, protect the individual and correct errors
Quietly remove the target and take no further steps

questions.prompt: Why is keeping a note of dates and responses useful?

options.text: It supports escalation and any later explanation
It replaces the need to raise concerns with a manager
Tribunal rules require notes before any report is made
It lets the press know what happened

items.title: L10: When a public body fails: layers of accountability
items.source: Cabinet Office, Corporate governance code for central government departments; Managing Public Money; National Audit Office reports
items.body: When an arm's length body suffers a serious failure, such as a major payment error or a data breach, responsibility is spread across layers, and each layer has a different kind of accountability. The board is accountable for the body's governance, strategy and risk oversight, and the chair is accountable to the sponsor minister for the board's effectiveness. The chief executive, as accounting officer, is accountable for the body's use of resources and delivery, and may be called before the Public Accounts Committee. The sponsor department's permanent secretary, as principal accounting officer, is accountable for the system of oversight that the department operates over the body, including whether risks were identified and escalated. The sponsor team should show it had monitored performance, held regular meetings and acted on warning signs. The minister is accountable to Parliament for the policy and framework, and for explaining what happened and what is being done. External audit and inspection bodies may examine too. The legal duties may vary: for instance, in a data breach, the body is the data controller and must notify the ICO. Consequences differ: the board may face criticism and changes of membership; a chief executive may be held to account through the board or be asked to step down; the minister may face political consequences; and the department might have to change its sponsorship practices. A fair review looks at whether the failure came from a decision made at board level, from poor management, from policy or funding decisions, or from weak assurance. It also considers whether warnings were ignored or not passed on. Learning should be shared across government, for instance through reports and lessons-learned guidance. Statements to Parliament must be accurate and avoid claiming that the matter is 'for the body' when the department has oversight duties.

questions.prompt: Which layer is accountable for the body's governance, strategy and risk oversight?

options.text: The Treasury, which approves each body's governance arrangements
The board, with the chair answerable to the sponsor minister
The sponsor team alone, which runs the board
The National Audit Office, which sets the body's strategy

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for the system of oversight the sponsor department runs over the body?

options.text: The sponsor department's permanent secretary
The body's chief executive, who runs it day to day
The chair of the body, who leads the board
The Speaker, who oversees public bodies

questions.prompt: A data breach occurs. What is the body's role under data protection law?

options.text: It is only a data processor, with no duties of its own
It has no duties because it is part of government
The sponsor minister is the data controller instead
It is the data controller and must notify the ICO where required

questions.prompt: Which question belongs in a fair review?

options.text: Who was the most senior person involved
Who is most popular with staff
Whether warnings were ignored or not passed on
Which staff members are youngest in their roles

questions.prompt: A minister tells Parliament that a failure is 'a matter for the body' despite the department's oversight role. Why might this be wrong?

options.text: It may mislead by ignoring the department's oversight duties
It is always correct, because bodies are independent
Parliament cannot ask ministers about arm's length bodies
Ministers cannot refer to bodies in statements

questions.prompt: Which of these would show the sponsor team acted properly?

options.text: That it never met the body, to respect its independence
That it left all decisions to the board in every case
That it monitored, met regularly and acted on warnings
That it relied only on the body's annual report

questions.prompt: Which consequence can fall on the minister?

options.text: A prison sentence, which follows automatically from a failure
Dismissal by the board of the body
A fine from the National Audit Office
Political consequences and a duty to explain

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of sharing lessons across government?

options.text: It lowers the cost of external audits
Other bodies can avoid similar failures
It removes accountability from individual bodies
It prevents any inquiry from taking place

items.title: L10: Prioritising under pressure: law, equality and honesty together
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Code; Managing Public Money
items.body: Operational managers sometimes face situations in which law, fairness, resources and honesty all apply. Suppose a team faces a large backlog of claims, a statutory deadline for one category, a group of customers who are vulnerable and a new target set by senior managers. A multi-step approach helps. First, identify legal duties: statutory deadlines are not optional, and breaching them can lead to legal challenge or compensation, so they set the minimum. Second, identify risks to people: cases involving risk of harm, destitution or safeguarding are normally prioritised, even if they are not the oldest or quickest. Third, apply the public sector equality duty by checking whether the way work is being allocated disadvantages any group, for example by prioritising cases that can be done online, which may disadvantage people with limited digital access. Fourth, consider fairness and consistency: choose criteria that are written down and applied evenly. Fifth, deal honestly with data: the target should not be met by closing cases prematurely or moving them between queues to avoid measurement. Sixth, escalate: tell senior managers and ministers about the trade-offs, showing that meeting the target as set would require failing to meet a legal duty or harming vulnerable customers, and ask for a decision, extra resources or a changed target. Seventh, communicate honestly with customers about delays and offer routes for urgent cases. Eighth, record decisions so they can be explained to Parliament or a court. If a manager is told to meet the target regardless, they should record their advice, and if the instruction would require unlawful or dishonest action, raise it under the Code. Trade-offs need to be made explicit, and the person with authority should own them.

questions.prompt: A new target would be met only by delaying vulnerable customers' claims past a statutory deadline. What should the manager do?

options.text: Meet the target by delaying those claims and say nothing about the effect on customers
Ignore the target and carry on as before, without telling senior managers why
Set out the trade-off to senior managers and ask for resources or a decision
Delay only some of the vulnerable claims, to limit the damage and avoid the discussion

questions.hint: Trade-offs should be made explicit and owned.

questions.prompt: What do statutory deadlines set in a prioritisation decision?

options.text: A guideline that managers may set aside to meet a target
A target for average performance across the whole caseload
A preference that applies only to large or complex cases
A minimum that must be met whatever other targets say

questions.prompt: Which way of allocating work might breach the equality duty?

options.text: Prioritising only cases that can be done online
Prioritising cases by the risk of harm to the customer
Prioritising by written criteria applied evenly across teams
Prioritising by statutory deadline before other cases

questions.hint: Check whether an approach disadvantages a group.

questions.prompt: Why should prioritisation criteria be written down?

options.text: So that staff can choose freely which cases to take first
So decisions are consistent and can be explained later
So that training for new staff is no longer needed
So that the press can see how every case was dealt with

questions.prompt: A manager is told to meet the target regardless of the effect. What should they do?

options.text: Record their advice, and raise it under the Code if unlawful
Comply without comment, since senior managers are responsible for targets
Resign at once, so as not to be party to any breach
Tell the press that the target is unreasonable and cannot be met

questions.prompt: Which action would breach the honesty value?

options.text: Telling customers about delays and how to ask for urgent handling
Recording the reasons for prioritisation decisions
Asking senior managers for extra resources
Moving cases between queues so they escape measurement

questions.prompt: What should customers be told when a backlog builds?

options.text: That there are no delays, to avoid complaints and extra contact
Honest information about delays and how to ask for urgent help
That any delay is caused by customers who applied late
Nothing, until a customer complains about waiting

questions.prompt: Why record prioritisation decisions at the time?

options.text: So that the department meets a Cabinet Office reporting target
So that they can be published on GOV.UK each month
So they can be explained later to Parliament or a court
So that audit teams have less to review

items.title: L10: Designing an arm's length body
items.source: Cabinet Office, Public Bodies Reform and Classification of public bodies; Public Bodies Reform: Proposals for Change (2010)
items.body: Deciding how to deliver a function involves choosing between several organisational forms, each with different levels of independence and control. A function can stay in a ministerial department, which gives ministers direct control and accountability. It can be placed in an executive agency, which stays part of the department but has a chief executive and a framework document giving operational freedom within agreed targets. It can be a non-ministerial department, headed by a board or a statutory office-holder, which is not under direct ministerial direction but is still a government department. It can be an executive non-departmental public body, which has its own legal identity and board, receives public funding, and carries out functions at arm's length from ministers. It can be an advisory body, which provides expert advice but does not decide. It can also be a public corporation or an independent regulator. The Cabinet Office's review in 2010 suggested three tests for a body to exist outside a department: it performs a technical function that requires external expertise; its activity requires political impartiality, for example regulation or adjudication; or it needs to act independently to establish facts. If none of these applies, the default is to keep the function in a department. Considerations include accountability: more independence means ministers have less direct control but still answer to Parliament for the framework; costs and capability; need for flexibility in recruitment and pay; and public trust. Setting up a body needs legislation if it is to have statutory powers or independence. Decision-makers should also plan governance: a board, an accounting officer, clear funding and reporting arrangements. They should plan reviews so that the arrangement can be updated if it no longer meets the tests. Changing form is costly, so the decision needs careful analysis and the minister's agreement.

questions.prompt: A function sets technical standards that need external expertise and independence from political pressure. Which form is most likely to be justified?

options.text: A ministerial department, because it keeps direct control for ministers
An arm's-length body, since it meets the Cabinet Office tests
A unit within the Prime Minister's private office, for speed
A local council, because local bodies are independent of ministers

questions.hint: The tests point to arm's length.

questions.prompt: A function does not meet any of the three tests. What is the default?

options.text: Create a non-departmental public body to carry it out
Create a regulator with statutory independence
Create an advisory body to consider the issue
Keep it in a department

questions.hint: Without a justification, it stays in a department.

questions.prompt: Which form stays part of a department but has a chief executive and a framework document?

options.text: An executive agency
An advisory non-departmental public body
A public corporation
An independent regulator

questions.hint: Agencies are part of their departments.

questions.prompt: What does moving a function to an independent body do to ministerial accountability?

options.text: Ministers have no accountability for the body, so Parliament cannot ask them
Ministers gain full control over each decision the body takes
Ministers have less direct control but still answer for the framework
Parliament loses the right to question the body's chief executive

questions.prompt: When is legislation likely to be needed to set up a body?

options.text: Always, whatever form is chosen
Never, because the Crown can create bodies by decision
Only for advisory bodies, which give advice to ministers
When it needs statutory powers or statutory independence

questions.prompt: Which governance arrangements should be planned for a new body?

options.text: A chief executive only, with no board to slow decisions
A board, an accounting officer and clear reporting lines
Direct reporting to the Treasury only, with no sponsor department
A committee of ministers to take each operational decision

questions.prompt: Why plan periodic reviews of an arm's length body?

options.text: Its form may no longer be justified
To reduce its budget over time as the body becomes established
To avoid the need for annual reports and accounts
To replace the board every few years with new members

questions.prompt: Why is changing the form of a body costly?

options.text: It is not costly, since staff simply move across
It needs only a press release to change the form
It involves legal change and disruption
It does not affect staff or contracts

items.title: L10: From idea to delivery: sign-off and accountability
items.source: Cabinet Manual; HM Treasury, Green Book and Managing Public Money; Cabinet Office guidance on policy-making
items.body: Follow a policy from idea to delivery to see how decisions, sign-offs and accountabilities connect. A minister proposes a new scheme. Officials first develop options, using evidence and appraisal under the Green Book. They consult other departments with an interest, including the Treasury, which must agree to any new spending or commitments. If the policy affects devolved matters, they engage the devolved governments. If it is significant or cross-cutting, it goes to a Cabinet committee for collective agreement. If primary legislation is needed, a Bill is prepared with Parliamentary Counsel, introduced and passed, and secondary legislation made under it. Business cases are developed through strategic, outline and full stages, with Treasury approval at set thresholds. The accounting officer must be satisfied that the proposal meets the four standards. The Equality Act duty requires consideration of the effects on different groups, and the data protection impact assessment checks privacy risks. Procurement, if needed, follows public procurement law. Delivery is planned: a senior responsible owner, programme governance, risk management and benefits tracking. If the scheme is delivered through an agency or arm's length body, the framework document and funding must reflect it. During delivery, officials monitor progress, report to the minister and the board, and escalate risks. After delivery, evaluation takes place, informed by the Magenta Book. Throughout, accountability is layered: ministers answer to Parliament for policy; the accounting officer for the use of resources; the senior responsible owner for delivery; and chief executives for operations. Parliament scrutinises through questions, select committees and the NAO. If a stage is skipped, risks increase, for example in unfunded commitments or unlawful actions.

questions.prompt: A new scheme needs primary legislation. Which sequence is closest to the correct order?

options.text: Appraise, agree across government, pass the Bill, then deliver
Delivery, then legislation, then appraisal of the results
The Bill is passed, then options are appraised and the Treasury consulted
Consultation after Royal Assent, then Treasury consent

questions.prompt: Which body must agree to new spending commitments?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary, who controls all departmental budgets
The Treasury
The Speaker, who authorises spending each year
The National Audit Office, which approves new commitments

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for the use of resources in the scheme?

options.text: The senior responsible owner alone
The Speaker, on behalf of Parliament
The Treasury minister, for each department
The accounting officer

questions.prompt: Which role is accountable for delivery of a programme?

options.text: The accounting officer for all matters of delivery
The select committee overseeing the department
The senior responsible owner
The Prime Minister's private office

questions.prompt: The scheme affects devolved matters. What should be done during development?

options.text: Wait until the scheme is announced and then inform them
Engage them early and seek consent where needed
Tell their parliaments after Royal Assent
Leave them out, since policy is a UK matter

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the data protection impact assessment?

options.text: To satisfy the Treasury before funding is approved
To approve the budget for the scheme
To find and reduce privacy risks to individuals
To decide which legislative route to use

questions.prompt: If a stage such as Treasury agreement is skipped, what risk increases?

options.text: Unfunded commitments and later challenge
Extra risk is small, since the Treasury will sort out any gaps later
Speed will fall, which is the only real risk
The scheme becomes more popular with the public

questions.prompt: What does the Magenta Book inform?

options.text: Procurement of suppliers for the programme
Drafting of Bills with Parliamentary Counsel
Preparing answers to parliamentary questions
Evaluation after or during delivery

items.title: L10: Official resources and the line between government and party
items.source: Ministerial Code; Code of Conduct for Special Advisers; Civil Service Code; GCS Propriety Guidance
items.body: Applying the line between government business and party business needs judgement because the two often overlap. Ministers are both members of the government and members of a political party, and they are entitled to do party work, but not with public resources. Officials need to understand what falls on each side. Government business includes policy development, explaining policy to the public, answering Parliament, and running the department. Party business includes campaigning, party conferences, preparing party manifestos, and attacking opponents. Public resources include staff time, premises, equipment, official cars, department budgets, and official social media. A minister's private office handles diary entries, but they should not manage party events in office hours. Special advisers can do party-political work, within the Code of Conduct, but they must use party resources for party-only tasks. Visits are a frequent grey area: a ministerial visit to a factory to see a government scheme is official, but if it is arranged to feature a local candidate during an election campaign, it may stray. Speeches are mixed: an official speech should explain policy, while party conference speeches are party business and should be prepared without official staff. Press releases from the department must not be party political; a minister's party press release should be issued from party channels. Where something has both purposes, costs may need to be apportioned and the party should pay for the party element. If officials are asked to do something on the party side, they should decline politely, explain the rule and suggest alternative routes. If doubts remain, they can consult the permanent secretary's office or the propriety and ethics team. Record keeping is useful. Officials should be consistent whichever party is in power.

questions.prompt: A minister asks the private office to arrange a party fundraising dinner in office hours using the office diary. What is the proper response?

options.text: Decline politely, explain that party business cannot use official resources
Arrange it as a courtesy, since the minister has asked and it is only a diary entry
Arrange it but record it as a departmental event so the time can be justified
Arrange it provided that the minister agrees to pay for the room

questions.prompt: A visit to see a government scheme is arranged to feature a local candidate in the middle of an election campaign. What is the concern?

options.text: None, since ministers may visit anywhere they choose
None, provided photographs are taken for the department
None, if the candidate is also a minister
It could slip from government business into campaigning

questions.prompt: Where should a minister's party-political press release be issued from?

options.text: The department's press office, as the minister is its head
GOV.UK, where all ministerial statements are published
Party channels, not the department's press office
The permanent secretary's office, to give it authority

questions.prompt: Which of the following may a special adviser do?

options.text: Direct departmental staff to prepare party leaflets
Prepare party material using party resources
Give orders to civil servants about their duties
Run the department's budget for the minister

questions.hint: Spads handle party tasks within their Code.

questions.prompt: A speech has policy explanation and party attack lines. What is the best approach?

options.text: Have officials draft the whole speech, including the attack lines
Refuse to support any speech by that minister
Officials do the explanation and party staff the rest
Draft it all, but mark the attack lines as draft only

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to ask whether the same request would be proper if the other party were in office?

options.text: It tells officials what the opposition would want
It tests consistency with impartiality
It is a legal test set out in the Equality Act
It lets the minister choose the outcome

questions.prompt: Where can officials seek advice on whether something is government or party business?

options.text: The propriety and ethics team
The opposition's office, since it is neutral
The press, who often know the rules
A friend in another department

questions.prompt: If an activity has both government and party purposes, what may need to happen to the costs?

options.text: The department pays all of them, since the minister is in government
The party pays none, as it is a government event
The Treasury pays the difference
Apportioned, with the party paying for its element

items.title: L10: Building a defensible decision record
items.source: Civil Service Code; Judicial Review Handbook; National Archives, Records management guidance
items.body: A decision that cannot be explained is hard to defend, however good it was. When officials must make an important decision, such as refusing an application, awarding a contract or changing a policy, a good record allows others to see how it was made and why. The core elements are: the decision-maker, their authority and the date; the question to be decided; the legal and policy framework; the evidence considered, including any that cut against the decision; the options; the reasons for choosing one; the consultation or representations received and how they were weighed; and the equality and data protection implications. The reasoning should show that relevant factors were considered and irrelevant ones were not. Contemporaneous notes carry more weight than reconstructed accounts. The record should be honest about uncertainty and assumptions, and should not include speculation or inappropriate comments, because it may be disclosed through FOI, subject access, a tribunal or judicial review. Legal advice should be kept separately and clearly marked as privileged. Decisions should be taken by someone with delegated authority, and sign-off should follow the department's process. Where a decision departs from policy or earlier practice, the reasons for the departure should be recorded. Where timescales are short, a brief record at the time, with more detail later, is better than none. Records should be saved in the right place, with clear titles and version control, and linked to the case. After the decision, communication to affected people should explain it clearly, including routes for review or appeal. Records should be retained according to the schedule and not destroyed when litigation is possible. Where a record is wrong, it should be corrected with an annotation, and the original kept, not overwritten.

questions.prompt: Which element makes a decision record most defensible?

options.text: A long description of the decision-maker's feelings about the case
A copy of the press release that announced the decision
A signature alone, to show who approved it
Reasons showing relevant factors were weighed, irrelevant ones not

questions.prompt: An official reconstructs the reasoning for a decision three months afterwards. What is the weakness?

options.text: None, since reconstructed accounts are accepted as they are
Contemporaneous notes carry more weight than later accounts
Reconstructed accounts are unlawful
Notes are unnecessary if the decision-maker remembers the case

questions.prompt: A record contains speculative personal remarks about an applicant. What is the risk?

options.text: It may later be disclosed or tested in court
None, since records are private to the department
It will be checked by the minister before release
It improves the record by showing candour

questions.hint: Write as if it will be disclosed.

questions.prompt: Where timescales are short, what is the best practice?

options.text: Records left until time permits, and then written in full
A record only if a complaint arises
A brief note at the time, with detail added later
A verbal agreement, confirmed later by email

questions.hint: Something recorded at the time is better than nothing.

questions.prompt: A decision departs from earlier practice. What should the record show?

options.text: The reasons for the departure
Nothing, since the decision-maker has discretion
A copy of the earlier practice only
The press view of the departure

questions.prompt: A record contains a factual error. How should it be corrected?

options.text: By deleting the original and replacing it
By overwriting it silently
By annotation, keeping the original record
By leaving it as it is, since it is only a record

questions.prompt: Where should legal advice relating to the decision be kept?

options.text: In the main case file with no marking
Separately, marked as privileged
In the decision-maker's personal email
In the press office files for reference

questions.prompt: What should be done with records when litigation is possible?

options.text: Destroy them under the schedule as normal
Move them to personal storage for safety
Edit them to remove errors
Keep them and suspend routine destruction

items.title: L10: Weighing duties when everything points different ways
items.source: Civil Service Code; Ministerial Code; Managing Public Money; Nolan Principles
items.body: Hard cases often involve several duties at once. A structured way of thinking helps. First, identify the facts and what is known and not known. Second, identify which duties apply: legal duties to follow the law, Code values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, accountability to ministers, duties to Parliament, the accounting officer's four tests, data protection and confidentiality, and duties to colleagues and the public. Third, ask whether the duties conflict, or only seem to. Many apparent conflicts disappear when facts are clarified or when an alternative is found, such as providing a minister with the information in a form that protects confidentiality. Fourth, rank by seriousness: legal duties and honesty are not negotiable and cannot be traded for speed or loyalty. Merits of policy are for ministers. Questions of timing, handling and style often allow flexibility. Fifth, consider consequences: who could be harmed, how likely and how severe, and whether the harm is reversible. Sixth, identify the least drastic option that respects the duties, such as raising the issue, seeking advice, or proposing an alternative, before more serious steps. Seventh, consult: line manager, nominated officer, legal and propriety advisers. Eighth, record the reasoning. Ninth, be prepared to explain it to someone who disagrees, including Parliament. The Nolan Principles of selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership provide a check. Leadership means taking responsibility for acting on the right course and encouraging others to do so. If after all this the outcome is still uncertain, officials can escalate for a decision by someone with the right authority. They should not freeze. Good judgement shows in the quality of the reasoning and the care taken to find a way that respects all the duties, not in always avoiding risk.

questions.prompt: A minister asks for confidential information about a named person held by another department. The duty to the minister seems to conflict with data protection. What should the official do first?

options.text: Check for a lawful basis or anonymised alternative first
Hand it over, since ministers' requests outrank data protection rules
Refuse without discussion, since data protection rules always apply
Send it to the press office to decide on release

questions.hint: Seek an alternative that respects both.

questions.prompt: Which duties cannot be traded for speed or loyalty?

options.text: The style in which advice is drafted
The timing of announcements
Legal duties and honesty
The format of papers

questions.prompt: Which matter is for ministers rather than officials?

options.text: Whether the law applies to a decision
The merits of a policy
Whether records are kept honestly
Whether to mislead Parliament

questions.prompt: How should an official choose between possible responses to a dilemma?

options.text: Pick the most dramatic response, to show how serious the concern is
Pick the quickest response, to avoid delay
Pick the one that avoids discussion with anyone else
Choose the least drastic option that respects the duties

questions.prompt: Which consideration affects how cautious to be?

options.text: How many people already know about the issue
Whether it is likely to be reported in the news
How likely and severe the harm is
Which day of the week the decision falls on

questions.prompt: If uncertainty remains after careful analysis, what should officials do?

options.text: Do nothing, in case acting makes matters worse
Escalate to someone with authority, and not freeze
Wait to see whether the problem resolves itself
Choose the option that is least likely to be noticed

questions.prompt: Who should be consulted in hard cases?

options.text: Only the press office, which knows how it will look
Only close friends in other teams
Only the suppliers or customers concerned
Line manager, nominated officer, propriety advisers

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes good judgement in these cases?

options.text: Careful reasoning that respects every duty
It means always saying no to avoid risk
It means always following what the minister prefers
It means avoiding any written record of the difficulty
